Getting started¶

This chapter takes you through four things: getting the program, a single-point energy of water, a geometry optimization of ammonia followed by a Hessian that proves the structure is a minimum, and the parts of the output you need to read along the way. Installing and running covers running the program in more detail.

The example inputs were run on Priroda 25 (2025.02.28), and most output excerpts are copied from those runs. A few excerpts come from outputs posted by users of older versions; the text says so where it matters.

Obtaining Priroda¶

Priroda is free of charge. Everything you need to run it can be downloaded from the official site, https://rad.chem.msu.ru/~laikov/p_w/: the executables, the basis-set files and the helper scripts. Put the executable and basis.in in a directory of your own. The main Linux executable, p, is statically linked, so a serial run needs no other libraries. The page is a bare file index with no documentation, license text or contact information. It holds:

  • Linux x86-64 executables (p, p4, p_d, p4_d), builds for particular clusters (p_l, p_mvs1p1, p_mvs10p, p_mvs10q), an ARM build (p_arm), a bundled mpiexec, and the molecule viewer xm;

  • Windows (Cygwin, x86-64) executables in exe64/;

  • example inputs and outputs;

  • basis-set and parameter files (basis.in, basis4.in, b2*.in, b4s*.in, 3z.bas, sbk.bas, qm.in);

  • small shell scripts: ge (append the $Energy block from an output to the input), gm (replace $molecule with the optimized geometry) and grx (join two IRC halves).

Which executable to choose is described in Installing and running. For the examples in this chapter you need one Linux executable (for example p) and basis.in.

Users have also obtained the program by writing to the developer, Dimitri Laikov, by e-mail. Users reported the address dimitri_laikov@mail.ru from 2010 to 2018; earlier it was laikov@physto.se. Users note that he does not always answer quickly.

Note

The legal status is not stated on the official site. A 2009 presentation relayed on a forum said that Priroda is registered with Rospatent and distributed through the company OOO “Dimonta”. A user reported in 2018 that the developer had said, a couple of years earlier, that there was no licence agreement. Users customarily ask the developer’s permission before using the program.

The official site has hosted builds with known defects. In 2016 it carried a note that the w64/*.exe builds (an attempt at 64-bit Cygwin) had a DFT/ECP bug. If a build behaves strangely, ask the developer whether it is the right one.

Before you start¶

Four practical points save most first-time failures.

  • Plain text with Unix line endings. Write inputs as plain ASCII with LF line endings and straight quotes. A file saved with Windows (CRLF) line endings gives errors such as molecule input: '' or ?rtesian, or makes task=scan silently run an optimization. Convert such files with dos2unix.

  • Give the basis file by its full path. The basis keyword names the basis-set file. A relative name works in version 25 when the file is in the directory you run from, but relative names have failed in older versions and in parallel runs, so an absolute path is the safe choice. The examples below use /home/user/priroda/basis.in; replace it with the location of basis.in on your machine.

  • Atomic numbers are integers. Each atom line in $molecule starts with the atomic number written as an integer (8, not 8.0 and not O). A real number such as 8.0 gives no error: the program silently reads a different molecule.

  • Running. A serial run is p input output. Parallel runs are described in Installing and running.

A single-point energy¶

The input¶

Save the following as water.in:

$system mem=128 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=energy
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
 print=+charges+bonds
$end
$dft functional=PBE $end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 cartesian
 set=L1
  8    0.000000    0.000000    0.117300
  1    0.000000    0.757200   -0.469200
  1    0.000000   -0.757200   -0.469200
$end

Group by group:

  • $system sets the memory limit in MB and the scratch space. Here disk=1 means 1 GB of disk for temporary files; a negative value would mean a RAM disk of that many MB. These values are per process.

  • $control sets the job type and the method. task=energy asks for the energy at the given geometry. theory=dft is GGA DFT with density fitting, the program’s standard method. print=+charges+bonds adds Hirshfeld charges and Mulliken populations to the output (see Charges and bond orders below).

  • $dft selects the functional. PBE is already the default, so this line only makes the choice visible.

  • $molecule holds the charge, the multiplicity (2S+1), the geometry, and the basis set. The geometry is given in Cartesian coordinates (Å), one line per atom: atomic number, then x, y, z. set=L1 picks the set named L1 from basis.in. L1 is also the default set of that file, and users compare it to cc-pVDZ in size.

Note

Hybrid functionals such as PBE1 or B3LYP need theory=ridft. With theory=dft, older versions silently drop the exact exchange, and newer ones abort with no error message. See $control theory.

Run it:

p water.in water.out

What to look for in the output¶

The excerpts below are from this input run on Priroda 25. The output starts with the version banner, Priroda 25 (2025.02.28), and the memory and disk limits. The line molecule input: '' follows in every run; it is not an error. Then come the coordinates, the formula: line and a table of interatomic distances. Check the formula: it is the quickest way to catch a misread $molecule group.

Next, a summary box repeats what the program understood from your input. Check that the charge, multiplicity, method and functional are what you meant:

 +---------------------------------------
 | Number of atoms                      3
 | Charge of molecule                   0
 | Spin multiplicity                    1
 | Number of alpha electrons            5
 | Number of beta  electrons            5
 | Number of core  electrons            1
 | Theoretical Method                 DFT
 | Approximation to E(xc)             PBE
 | Dimension of wavefunction basis     24
 | Dimension of   auxiliary  basis     50
 | Hamiltonian: non-relativistic
 +---------------------------------------

The electron counts are per spin. “Number of core electrons” counts core orbitals (here the oxygen 1s); it matters only for correlated methods.

Two lines then echo the SCF and grid settings, including defaults you did not set:

 scf: conv = 1.0e-06, 1.0e-03; iter=32,16; xmax = 0.25000; 0s; n1=12
 grid: accuracy=1.0e-08,1.0e-05, cut=1.0e-10,1.0e-07, t=-1

Next comes the SCF iteration table (columns for the energy, the energy change and the gradient, with indented micro-iterations). The grid is enlarged partway through, which is why the energy jumps once. A successful SCF ends with the line converged!.

Warning

If the SCF fails, the program prints no convergence! (or, in older versions, SCF is far from convergence) and then carries on: it prints an energy, orbitals and properties, and exits normally. The numbers are not usable. Always look for converged! before trusting a result; Solving common problems lists the fixes.

The total energy follows, in hartree, on the line starting with E  =, together with its components:

  E  =     -76.3653913723
  T  =      76.07611549  V  =    -199.28820003  J  =      46.93680394
  Ex =      -8.95038631  Ec =      -0.32925888

  dipole =   0.735449 au (  1.869339 D)

If your energy differs from this one in more than the last few digits, check the basis file and the version.

E is the number you want. The components T, V, J, Ex and Ec do not add up to E, because the nuclear repulsion energy is not printed on these lines. This is expected and is not an error.

Every run also prints its results as a restart block on lines prefixed with eng>. For task=energy it holds the energy and the dipole moment; gradient and Hessian runs add more:

eng>$Energy
eng> E=-7.6365391372338e+01
eng> D=-2.96281302e-14  6.81315681e-13 -7.35448725e-01
eng>$end

Optimizing a geometry and confirming a minimum¶

The standard beginner procedure, as taught on the KNC wiki, alternates between optimizations and Hessians:

  1. Optimize the geometry.

  2. Check that the optimization converged. If it did not, restart from the last geometry.

  3. Take the final geometry and compute a Hessian (force constants and vibrational frequencies) there.

  4. If any frequency is imaginary, the structure is not a minimum: re-optimize with that Hessian in the input, then compute a new Hessian.

  5. When all frequencies are real, read the thermochemistry.

The Hessian check matters most when the start geometry is symmetric. An experienced user reports that Priroda’s optimizer rarely leaves imaginary frequencies, except when the starting structure is symmetric and the optimizer keeps that symmetry; then the check is compulsory.

Step 1: optimize¶

Save the following as nh3.in:

$system mem=128 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=optimize
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
$end
$optimize tol=1e-5 steps=100 $end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 z-matrix
 set=L1
   7
   1    1    1.02672223
   1    1    1.02672140    2    104.150240
   1    1    1.02671372    2    104.144601   -3    104.150290
$end

The third hydrogen is placed by one distance and two angles: the negative index -3 means “the angle to atom 3” instead of a dihedral.

tol is the convergence threshold on the gradient. The displacement threshold is then set to 100 times that value. The default is 1e-4; the tighter 1e-5 used in most published examples is a better starting point for a Hessian. steps caps the number of cycles (128 by default in version 25; older versions used 50). If an optimization needs far more than 50 steps, raising the limit rarely helps; supplying a Hessian usually does. The output echoes all these settings under Geometry optimization options:.

Run it with p nh3.in nh3.out.

Step 2: check convergence¶

Each optimization cycle starts with a line such as Geometry Optimization Step 1:, followed by the energy, the largest gradient and the largest displacement. When both are below the thresholds, the program prints OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED in N steps!. Check for it:

grep "OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED" nh3.out

Right after the marker, the program prints the optimized geometry as a ready-made $molecule group, each line prefixed with MOL>, followed by the final energy. For nh3.in, version 25 printed:

 OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED in 6 steps!
MOL>$molecule
MOL> z-matrix
MOL> set=L1
MOL>   7
MOL>   1    1    1.02753254
MOL>   1    1    1.02744669    2    104.120811
MOL>   1    1    1.02748748    2    104.112983   -3    104.135802
MOL>$end
MOL> Energy =    -56.4988651558

The block keeps the coordinate type of the input: a Z-matrix input gives a Z-matrix with the optimized values. Only a charge or multiplicity that differs from the defaults (0 and 1) is written: nh3.in gives no such line, and an OH⁻ optimization gave MOL> charge=-1. So the block can be pasted into the next input as it is.

Step 3: take the final geometry¶

Strip the MOL> prefix to get a group you can paste into the next input. The following commands copy nh3.in to nh3_freq.in, switch the task to hessian, drop the old $molecule group and everything after it, and append the optimized geometry:

sed -e 's/task=optimize/task=hessian/' -e '/\$molecule/,$d' nh3.in > nh3_freq.in
sed -n 's/^MOL>//p' nh3.out >> nh3_freq.in

The first command assumes that $molecule is the last group of the input, as in all examples here. The Energy = ... line that ends up after $end does no harm: text outside a group is ignored. A normal optimization prints the MOL> block only once. A scan or an IRC prints one per point, so there you would pick the block you need.

Note

If the optimization did not converge, there are no MOL> lines, and the program prints no message about it: the output just ends after the last step. Do not restart from the original geometry: start from the last one reached. Every step prints the geometry for the next step as a $molecule group on lines prefixed with lower-case mol>, so this keeps the last such block:

sed -n 's/^mol>//p' nh3.out | awk '/\$molecule/{buf=""} {buf=buf $0 "\n"} END{printf "%s", buf}'

The official gm script (below) falls back to the input echo (lines starting with <$molecule) when there are no MOL> lines.

The official helper scripts ge and gm¶

The download site ships two small bash scripts for exactly this loop. Both take a job name (with or without the .in or .out extension) and work on name.in and name.out in place:

  • gm nh3 replaces the $molecule group in nh3.in with the optimized one from nh3.out and keeps the old input as nh3.bak. Like the commands above, it requires $molecule to be the last group, because it replaces everything from $molecule onwards. It also appends the final Energy = line and, when non-zero, the dipole line.

  • ge nh3 appends the eng> lines of nh3.out (the $Energy group: energy, gradient and, after a Hessian run, the Hessian) to the end of nh3.in.

So a cycle with these scripts is: run, gm, edit the task, run again. Note that ge copies every eng> line in the output, so use it on a Hessian output, not on an optimization output that has one block per step.

Step 4: compute the Hessian¶

After step 3, nh3_freq.in looks like this, with your optimized values in place of these coordinates. Two optional lines are added here: print=+molden (for viewing the vibrations, see Viewing results in Molden) and a $thermo group:

$system mem=128 disk=1 $end
$control
 task=hessian
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
 print=+molden
$end
$optimize tol=1e-5 steps=100 $end
$thermo sigma=3 $end
$molecule
 charge=0 mult=1
 z-matrix
 set=L1
   7
   1    1    1.02672223
   1    1    1.02672140    2    104.150240
   1    1    1.02671372    2    104.144601   -3    104.150290
$end

The $optimize group is ignored by a Hessian run but does no harm, and it is useful again if you have to go back to step 1. sigma is the rotational symmetry number used in the thermochemistry; for ammonia (point group C3v) it is 3. Priroda does not work it out itself: without sigma= it uses 1, and the entropy comes out too large by R ln σ (2.18 cal/(mol·K) for ammonia). The default temperature is 298.15 K; other temperatures go in temperature.

For DFT the Hessian is analytic; the output announces it with ANALYTIC SECOND DERIVATIVES OF SCF ENERGY.

Step 5: check the frequencies¶

For a minimum, all frequencies must be real (positive). A single imaginary frequency marks a transition state; several mean a higher-order saddle point. The frequencies are in the table after the line Harmonic Frequencies. For ammonia, version 25 printed:

 *------*---------*--------*---------*---------*--------*-----------*-----------*
 | Mode | Freq.   | Mass.  | IR Int. |Raman A. |Raman D.| ROA (90)  | ROA (180) |
 *------*---------*--------*---------*---------*--------*-----------*-----------*
 |    1 | 1095.36 |   1.18 | 111.670 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |
 |    2 | 1635.36 |   1.06 |  12.058 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |
 |    3 | 1635.49 |   1.06 |  12.054 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |
 |    4 | 3371.36 |   1.03 |   3.443 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |
 |    5 | 3488.82 |   1.09 |   0.493 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |
 |    6 | 3488.95 |   1.09 |   0.494 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |
 *------*---------*--------*---------*---------*--------*-----------*-----------*

The columns are the frequency in cm⁻¹, the reduced mass in amu and the IR intensity in km/mol. The Raman columns stay zero in a plain Hessian run; Raman intensities need task=dipole. A second table, Normal Modes (mass-weighted) and Frequencies, follows with the mode vectors. To print the table:

grep -A 12 "Harmonic Frequencies" nh3_freq.out

An imaginary frequency is printed with a trailing i. Planar ammonia, the transition state of the inversion, gives one:

 |    1 |  845.22i|   1.21 | 357.748 |   0.000 | 0.0000 |   0.00000 |   0.00000 |

grep "i|" nh3_freq.out therefore finds the imaginary modes.

Step 6: if a frequency is imaginary, re-optimize¶

Put the Hessian you just computed into the optimization input. It is printed as a $Energy group on eng> lines. Starting from a good Hessian, the optimizer can move off the saddle point; one extra cycle is usually enough.

sed -e 's/task=hessian/task=optimize/' nh3_freq.in > nh3_opt2.in
sed -n 's/^eng>//p' nh3_freq.out | awk '/\$Energy/{buf=""} {buf=buf $0 "\n"} END{printf "%s", buf}' >> nh3_opt2.in

The second command appends only the last $Energy group, after $molecule. Do not leave an older $Energy group in the file. Then run nh3_opt2.in and go back to step 2. (ge nh3_freq does the appending in place, if you work with the official scripts.)

Step 7: read the thermochemistry¶

Once all frequencies are real, the end of the Hessian output holds the zero-point energy and a table of thermodynamic functions. The KNC wiki points to the string ZPVE. Version 25 prints the table at 298.150 K by default; this older user output (molecule not stated) shows 298.000 K:

 E =  -196.328936    E0 =  -196.191669

 ZPVE = 0.137267 a.u. =   86.1366 kcal/mol

 ----------------------------------------------------------------------
 T =  298.000 K      ln(Q)       S          U          H          G
                              cal/mol*K  kcal/mol   kcal/mol   kcal/mol
 ----------------------------------------------------------------------
 translational      16.9514    38.6542     0.8883     1.4805   -10.0385
 rotational         11.1465    25.1313     0.8883     0.8883    -6.6008
 vibrational         0.6842     4.7490    87.1466    87.1466    85.7314
 total              28.7821    68.5345    88.9232    89.5154    69.0921
 ----------------------------------------------------------------------

How to read it:

  • E is the electronic energy in hartree. E0 = E + ZPVE is the energy corrected for the zero-point vibrational energy (here −196.328936 + 0.137267 = −196.191669).

  • The U, H and G columns are thermal corrections in kcal/mol, not total values. They already contain the ZPVE. The program does not print the total enthalpy or free energy; you add them yourself.

  • Take the corrections from the total row and add them to E, not E0. Adding them to E0 would count the zero-point energy twice:

    H = E + ddH, G = E + ddG, with ddH = H (total) and ddG = G (total).

  • Convert units before adding: 1 hartree = 627.51 kcal/mol. For the table above, G = −196.328936 × 627.51 + 69.0921 = −123129.28 kcal/mol, or −196.328936 + 69.0921 / 627.51 = −196.218831 hartree.

  • The entropy S (cal/(mol·K)) is taken from the total row as it stands.

Warning

For a single atom, the table is wrong: the rotational row contains -inf/inf or a spurious RT term. Use only the translational contribution for atoms. Older versions were also reported to put an extra RT into the enthalpy of monoatomic species.

The temperature is printed in the T = line. Version 25 uses 298.150 K; outputs posted by users of older versions also show 298.000 K. Set temperature explicitly when you compare results across versions.

The one-run alternative: task=optimize+hessian¶

You can let one job optimize the structure and then compute the Hessian at the converged geometry. In nh3.in, change the task line:

$control
 task=optimize+hessian
 theory=dft
 basis=/home/user/priroda/basis.in
 print=+molden
$end

This is the only combined task that works: two task= lines do not chain jobs, and only the first one runs. optimize+hessian existed in Priroda 2, was missing in versions 6 to 8, and is available again from version 9. If the resulting Hessian shows an imaginary frequency, you still need step 6.

Reading the output¶

Where things are¶

The output is plain text, and the results meant for reuse are on lines tagged with a prefix, so grep finds them.

Look for

What it is

the summary box (Number of atoms, Theoretical Method, …)

what the program understood from the input

converged! / no convergence!

the end of each SCF

E  =

total energy in hartree, followed by its components (without nuclear repulsion)

eng>

the $Energy group: energy E=, dipole D=, gradient G=, and the Hessian after task=hessian

OPTIMIZATION CONVERGED in N steps!

a converged optimization

MOL>

the optimized geometry as a $molecule group, then Energy =

Harmonic Frequencies

the frequency table (Normal Modes follows with the mode vectors)

ZPVE, T = ... K

zero-point energy and the thermochemistry table

Overlap populations:

Mulliken populations (print=+bonds)

Atomic partitions of the density:

Hirshfeld charges (print=+charges)

freq>

vibrations in Molden format (print=+molden, Hessian runs)

mos>

orbitals in Molden format (print=+vectors+molden)

Charges and bond orders¶

With print=+bonds, SCF runs print Mulliken charges and spin populations under Overlap populations:, followed by a table of bond orders. With print=+charges, DFT runs print Hirshfeld charges and spins under Atomic partitions of the density:. The flags can be combined, as in water.in, which gives:

 Overlap populations:
  atom    charge   spin p.
 O1      -0.4167  -0.00000
 H1       0.2083  -0.00000
 H2       0.2083  -0.00000

   Bond orders:
  O1    |  H1   :  1.07  H2   :  1.07
  H1    |  O1   :  1.07
  H2    |  O1   :  1.07

 Atomic partitions of the density:
   atom    charge    spin
   1  O   -0.2905    0.0000
   2  H    0.1451    0.0000
   3  H    0.1451    0.0000
  total   10.0003    0.0000

The total row of the Hirshfeld block sums the electron populations, not the charges.

Viewing results in Molden¶

The KNC wiki treats Molden as the reference viewer. Open files with the READ button in the Miscellaneous group.

Vibrations. Run the Hessian with print=+molden and cut out the freq> lines:

sed -n 's/^freq>//p' nh3_freq.out > nh3.freq

Open nh3.freq in Molden to animate the normal modes.

Orbitals. Add print=+vectors+molden to $control. The orbitals then appear on mos> lines:

grep '^mos>' water.out | sed 's/^mos>//' > water.mos

The +molden part is essential: without it, there are no mos> lines. The files are large, and Molden can be slow with them.

Geometry. If the optimized geometry is Cartesian, this one-liner turns the MOL> block into an XYZ file that Molden reads (the symbol list covers H to Ar; extend it for heavier elements):

sed -n 's/^MOL>//p' job.out | awk 'BEGIN{split("H He Li Be B C N O F Ne Na Mg Al Si P S Cl Ar",s," ")}
  NF==4 && $1+0>0 {n++; l[n]=s[$1]" "$2" "$3" "$4}
  END{print n; print "optimized geometry"; for(i=1;i<=n;i++) print l[i]}' > job.xyz

For a Z-matrix geometry such as nh3.in, the freq> file from the Hessian run is the easier way to look at the structure.

pri2mol. The Perl script pri2mol by the forum user amge, available from http://limor1.nioch.nsc.ru/quant/program/pri2mol/, converts a Priroda output into Molden and XYZ files: geometries, vibrations, orbitals, NMR shifts and density critical points. Priroda’s own viewer, xm, is on the download site.
